notes: Greylag Fold's goose-herd (pois/sedgemire.json); gives core:quest/the_unsung and takes its decision.

greetings.text: The girl is down there singing the first voice. Badly. The geese do not care that it is badly; they sleep. So do I, now.
They went out on the water singing, three hundred years of them, and the Vault is dark, and the carr is only a carr. I do not know if that is better. The geese sleep.
You still have it. I can see it on you even when it is in the pack. The geese face you now, all night, instead of the carr.
Quiet. I am on the third voice. If you must talk, talk under it.

greet.speaker: Eune Mor
greet.text: Stand still by the gate. They are coming in, and they will not come past a stranger who moves. — Forty-one. Thirty-eight. You see? Three short. The hounds, again. — Mor. Eune. This is the fold, and those are the geese, and that is my grandson, who cannot sing, pretending he can.

hub.speaker: Eune Mor
hub.text: Well. The geese are in. I can talk until they aren't.

choices.text: Why do the geese face west?
How do you bring them in?
The geese won't settle. Is there something I can do?
I have the Keeper's lantern.
I'll leave you to the geese.

west.speaker: Eune Mor
west.text: West is the carr. Under the carr is the Unsung Vault, where the drowned go that nobody will sing for, and a Keeper sings for all of them, every voice of the round, every night. Geese know a round. These were hatched under it. At the new moon it stopped, and they have stood facing it every night since and called, the way a goose calls for one that is missing from the skein.

singing.speaker: Eune Mor
singing.text: A goose follows a round it heard in the egg. You sing the first voice at the gate and they come in; you sing the second and they settle; you sing the third and they sleep. — I have been singing the third to the carr since the new moon. It is not the voice the carr wants. But it is a voice, and nobody else is.

q_the_unsung_offer.speaker: Eune Mor
q_the_unsung_offer.text: Something is wrong with the Keeper. — I cannot leave the geese, and my grandson cannot sing, and you have a sword, which in my experience is what people have instead. — The Keeper had a girl, a Sa, the second voice. She has been seen going into the Old Crannog at dusk. Find her. She will know what happened down there, and she will not want to say it.

choices.text: I'll find the girl at the crannog.
Not now.

q_the_unsung_accept.speaker: Eune Mor
q_the_unsung_accept.text: Go round the carr by the dry side. The hounds are in the reeds on the wet side, and they have had three of mine this week and would not mind a fourth.

q_the_unsung_decide.speaker: Eune Mor
q_the_unsung_decide.text: — Put it down. On the post, there, not on the ground. — That is the one. I saw it once when I was a girl, carried up the causeway for a Keeper's naming. It was lit then. It has been lit since before Isseva. — Every light in the Vault came off that one. Whatever is done with it is done to all of them. You carried it up. You say.

choices.text: Give it to Aue Sa. She can learn the first voice.
Take the unsung out to the water and sing them out, all of them.
I'm keeping it.
Let me think on it.

q_the_unsung_decide_aue_keeps.speaker: Eune Mor
q_the_unsung_decide_aue_keeps.text: The girl ran. — So did every Keeper, once, my mother said; the ones who never ran never came back up to be named. — I will take it to her myself, at dusk, singing the third. She will hear it coming, and know it is not the floor.

q_the_unsung_decide_sing_them_out.speaker: Eune Mor
q_the_unsung_decide_sing_them_out.text: All of them. — It will take every boat on the North Fen and every voice, and the geese will come too; they always come when there is singing. — Three hundred years. Then the carr is a carr. — Yes. Yes, I think that is what a round is for, in the end.

q_the_unsung_decide_keep_the_lantern.speaker: Eune Mor
q_the_unsung_decide_keep_the_lantern.text: — Then keep it. I will not take it off you; I am old and you have a sword. — But it will want the round, and you cannot give it the round. Remember I said so, when it starts to want.

bye.speaker: Eune Mor
bye.text: Go slowly past the gate. They count you too.

notes: Eune Mor's grandson at Greylag Fold.

greetings.text: They sleep now. All of them. Even Brass, who never sleeps, who I am not supposed to have named.

greet.speaker: Pello Mor
greet.text: Don't tell her I talked to you. She thinks talking unsettles them. — It doesn't. Singing badly unsettles them, and she won't let me sing, so I talk. That one is Brass. That one is Tollmere. That one is Grandmother, but don't tell her.

choices.text: What happened to your arm?
What's in the carr?
Goodbye, Pello.

arm.speaker: Pello Mor
arm.text: Leech-hound. Three nights ago, through the withies. I got it off Tollmere with the sling and it got me instead. — They come up out of the carr on the wet side. They didn't used to. The singing kept them down there with everything else, Grandmother says. Everything kept something down, in the old days.

carr.speaker: Pello Mor
carr.text: The Vault, and the old crannog, and nobody. — There's a girl sleeping in the crannog. I took her an egg. She hummed at me. It was the second voice, the one I can never find, and she got it right without trying, and then she stopped and said sorry, like it was something to be sorry for.

bye.speaker: Pello Mor
bye.text: Mind Brass. He bites people he likes.

notes: The Unsung Vault's runaway apprentice, at the Old Crannog (the crannog's 'somebody sleeps in it every night and leaves the fire laid'). core:quest/the_unsung's first stage closes on q_the_unsung_ran.

greetings.text: I am meant to be down there. I came up for the fire; I lay it every morning still. — I'm getting the first voice. The floor has stopped answering. I think it was only ever waiting for somebody to sing the right one.
Is she— did she go quiet? Properly quiet?

greet.speaker: Aue Sa
greet.text: — Sorry. I was humming. I do that. — Don't sit on the bed, nobody sleeps on the bed, it's a rule, nobody knows whose. — I'm not anybody. I'm just using the fire. I'll lay it again for the next one when I go.

choices.text: Eune Mor sent me. The singing under the carr has stopped.
Why does nobody sleep here twice?
What is the second voice?
I'll leave you the fire.

q_the_unsung_ran.speaker: Aue Sa
q_the_unsung_ran.text: — She sent you. Of course she did; she's been singing the third at me every night from the fold, did you know that? I can hear it from here. — I ran. — I was on the second voice, under the Keeper's first, the way I had been every night for six years. And she stopped. In the middle of a line. She stood there with her mouth open and her lantern up, and I kept going, because you keep going, and then I heard it. Under the floor. The second voice. Mine. Very nearly right. — And she was listening to it, not to me. And the lanterns started going out from the bottom, and the unsung started getting up out of the niches to hear, and I stopped singing, and I ran. — Her lantern is the first light. All the others came off it. If somebody put her to rest and brought it up into the day, it would— I don't know what it would. It would be up. Please.

twice.speaker: Aue Sa
twice.text: Because the crannog is older than stilts, and it remembers who slept in it, and it only has room to remember one of each. — That's what my grandmother said. I think it's because the bed is damp. — I sleep on the stones. And I don't sleep here twice. I sleep here every night, which is different, because I never wake up the same person who lay down.

second_voice.speaker: Aue Sa
second_voice.text: The round has three voices. The first leads, the second goes under it a line behind, the third comes in last and holds it. The dead can't sing any of them, so the living sing all three, and then the dead can go out. — In the Vault there was only the Keeper, so she sang the first and then went back and sang the second, and then the third, all night. And then there was me, for the second. — Now there's nobody. The fold is singing the third to nobody. It's the saddest thing I ever heard, and she's doing it on purpose.

bye.speaker: Aue Sa
bye.text: I'll lay the fire. For the next one. — Mind the stones on the causeway; three of them rock.

notes: Heron Watch's keeper (the bittern in its bell); gives core:quest/lanterns_taken_up and takes its decision.

greetings.text: Eighty-one lanterns went out from the shrine on one night. I counted them past the watch. All of them burned down before dawn, the way they should. I have knotted it. It is the longest knot on the rope.
The jetty-keepers are sending them out a few a night, each with its name, as they find it. It will take a year. That is right. A name takes as long as it takes.
— The bell tolled twice last night. — I have not knotted it. I do not know the knot for it. I do not want to.

greet.speaker: Tuo Lissa
greet.text: — … — Lissa. Tuo. — Stand off the ladder. She is on her nest in the bell and she does not know you, and I would rather she did not learn you by your hair.

choices.text: Why do you keep the watch?
What are the knots on the bell-rope?
You've been watching the channel at night.
I have the lanterns the Callers cut.
I'll leave you to the bittern.

the_watch.speaker: Tuo Lissa
the_watch.text: — … — It was raised to watch for the Lakefolk coming for the weir, when there were Lakefolk who came for weirs. Now it is where the young come to be alone together. — And I sit at the bottom so the young know somebody is at the bottom. And the bittern sits at the top. Between us nothing goes wrong.

the_rope.speaker: Tuo Lissa
the_rope.text: — … — Every night: what went up the channel, what came down, and whether the lanterns burned out right. A plain knot, nothing. A loop, a boat. A twist, a burial lantern going out as it should. — My grandmother taught me the knots. She went out under the Drowned Bell. — This month the rope is all loops going north, and no twists.

q_lanterns_taken_up_offer.speaker: Tuo Lissa
q_lanterns_taken_up_offer.text: — … — Boats. With no lanterns lit in them. A great many lanterns in them, unlit, stacked like baskets. Every night for a month, north up the Oulnauve. — The burial lanterns have been going dark on the water before they burn down, all over the Delta. You know what comes up when a lantern goes out early. — They sing in the boats. The Tide account. Backwards. — The Oulnauve bends round an old peat island two miles north. There is a palisade on it now. I would go. I am the watch; the watch does not go.

choices.text: I'll go up the Oulnauve.
Not now.

q_lanterns_taken_up_accept.speaker: Tuo Lissa
q_lanterns_taken_up_accept.text: — … — Bring the lanterns back if you can. Each one is a spoonful of oil for every year somebody lived. That is a great deal of years to leave in a heap.

q_lanterns_taken_up_decide.speaker: Tuo Lissa
q_lanterns_taken_up_decide.text: — … — Put them down. — Nine bundles of nine. Tagged for the Bell. — My grandmother went out under that bell. The diver says they are all standing round it on the bottom, waiting for it to say something. — Those lanterns are theirs. You carried them. What are they for?

choices.text: Light them and send them out again from the shrine, with the round.
Take them to the jetty at Isseva, to be sent out by name.
Sink them under the bell unlit. Let's see who comes up.
Let me think on it.

q_lanterns_taken_up_decide_light_and_sen.speaker: Tuo Lissa
q_lanterns_taken_up_decide_light_and_sen.text: — … — Tonight. All of them. I will come down off the watch for it, and the bittern can keep the channel. — Sing whichever voice you know. The dead do not mind which.

q_lanterns_taken_up_decide_to_isseva.speaker: Tuo Lissa
q_lanterns_taken_up_decide_to_isseva.text: — … — Yes. The jetty-keepers will know the frames, whose hand, which family. Every one with its own name, not in a heap. — That is slower. Slower is the reedfolk way. I should have thought of it.

q_lanterns_taken_up_decide_sink_them.speaker: Tuo Lissa
q_lanterns_taken_up_decide_sink_them.text: — … — You have been listening to the Callers. — Go. Do it, then; I cannot stop you, and I will not help. — I will knot it on the rope, whatever comes up. That is what the watch is for.

notes: Hester's House (a Vale cottage on a peat island); the Vale names on the Long Jetty are hers. Gives core:quest/names_from_the_vale and takes its decision.

greetings.text: On the water. — When it's time. Not before. I've barley to cut.
I went and stood by it. The hole. It's a good hole; somebody dug it square, the Vale way. I thanked it. Then I came home and planted another row.
There's my name on my own fence, lit, with all the others. In the Vale that'd be bad luck. On the water it's only company.

greet.speaker: Hester Wrenn
greet.text: You're from up the Westway. I can always tell; you walk like the ground's going to stay where you left it. — Sit on the step. It's a Vale step, it's meant for sitting. Hester Wrenn, of Gosford, and of here, which took longer.

hub.speaker: Hester Wrenn
hub.text: Go on, then. I've only the barley, and it isn't going anywhere.

choices.text: A Vale house, in the middle of the marsh?
Whose are the lanterns on the fence?
One lantern on your fence has no name.
I found where the lantern points.
I'll leave you to the barley.

the_house.speaker: Hester Wrenn
the_house.text: Tam built it. My husband. He came up to Gosford with a boat of eels on a cart, which is a thing I'd never seen, and I came back down with him, which he'd never seen either. He built me a house the Vale way, so I'd stay. Wattle and lime and thatch, on a peat island, and it's sinking an inch a year and I don't care. — He went into the water twenty years ago. I stayed anyway. Nobody was more surprised than me.

the_lanterns.speaker: Hester Wrenn
the_lanterns.text: Vale folk. The marsh drowns one every year or two: a carter who took the Greyreed in flood, a drover's girl come looking for her father, a runaway. They come to my door first, one way or another. The reedfolk would sing for them, but they wouldn't know the names. — So I make them a lantern, the way Tam's mother taught me, and write the name on it in Vale letters, and hang it on the Long Jetty, and the reedfolk sing the third voice for them without knowing why the letters look like that.

q_names_from_the_vale_offer.speaker: Hester Wrenn
q_names_from_the_vale_offer.text: — You noticed that. — It's for the one I've not had word of yet. There's always one more. — But that's not it. — Last week there was a lantern on the Long Jetty I didn't make. Last post, with mine. Reedfolk weave, Vale name. I saw it from the boat and I came home and I've not been out since. — Go and fetch it down for me. I'd rather read it here, on my own step, with the door behind me.

choices.text: I'll bring it from the jetty.
Not now.

q_names_from_the_vale_accept.speaker: Hester Wrenn
q_names_from_the_vale_accept.text: The Long Jetty's out on Lissane Mere, past Nauvissa. The drowned climb the last post at midnight; go by day. — And don't read it out there. Bring it home.

q_names_from_the_vale_decide.speaker: Hester Wrenn
q_names_from_the_vale_decide.text: — My name. — I knew it would be. Who else from the Vale is left down here to write? — And a grave on the hummock, dug square, the Vale way, with a board. And a burial lantern, the water way. — Somebody's done me both. Somebody who learned Vale letters to do it. — They've left me to choose. Or they've left you to. — Say it, then. I've been saying it to myself all week and I don't like the sound of my own voice on it.

choices.text: It means you're one of theirs. The water, when it's time.
It's the same kindness in Vale words. The earth, with the lantern beside it.
You're not dead. Hang it on your own fence and grow your barley.
Let me think on it.

q_names_from_the_vale_decide_the_water.speaker: Hester Wrenn
q_names_from_the_vale_decide_the_water.text: On the water. — Tam would laugh himself sick. — Forty years I've said in the Vale this and in the Vale that. — All right. On the water. With the round. And one of them can write my name in Vale letters on the paper, since somebody's learned how.

q_names_from_the_vale_decide_the_earth.speaker: Hester Wrenn
q_names_from_the_vale_decide_the_earth.text: The earth, and the lantern by it. Like Jonah Coe, and Tom with the Warden's buckle, and the rest of mine. — They dug it square. You know how long it takes a reedman to learn to dig square? Tam never did.

q_names_from_the_vale_decide_neither.speaker: Hester Wrenn
q_names_from_the_vale_decide_neither.text: — Ha. — Yes. — I'm not dead. I've a row to plant. — Give it here. It goes on the fence with the rest, lit, and when somebody passes and reads it they can think what they like.

bye.speaker: Hester Wrenn
bye.text: Mind the step. It's a Vale step; it's higher than you think.

notes: The Guild's clerk at the Eel Tally. Gives core:quest/tithe_day and takes its decision. The bravo on the steps is core:encounter/eel_tally (sits).

greetings.text: Forty barrels, paid back to Oulea out of the Guild's own chest. The Row sent me a letter about it. I have not opened it. I am enjoying not knowing.
The book agrees with itself now. That is what a book is for, the Row says. — Oulea's boat came in light this week. I did not ask.
They brought the stick. On tithe-day, in front of all three landings. I read it out. The bravo took his hand off his hilt. I have never been so frightened or so happy at a desk.

greet.speaker: Wystan Crail
greet.text: — four hundred and twelve, thirteen— Oh. Forgive me. I count. It's a habit, and it's the only one the Guild was ever pleased with. — Crail. Wystan Crail, clerk to the Guild at the Delta Tally. Don't touch the barrels; the gentleman on the steps is paid to mind that you don't.

hub.speaker: Wystan Crail
hub.text: What can the Guild do for you? Very little, I expect, but I'm obliged to ask.

choices.text: What is the Tally?
Who is the man on the steps?
You look like a man with a problem in a column.
I have the trappers' tally-stick.
Good day, clerk.

the_tally.speaker: Wystan Crail
the_tally.text: Every live eel that goes up to Tollmere from the Delta is counted here first. One in ten stays: the Guild's tithe, for the market, the road and the Charter. It's in the Charter. Everything is in the Charter. — The reedfolk pole their catch in, I chalk the barrels, I write the book. The eels do not care. I have come to envy them.

the_bravo.speaker: Wystan Crail
the_bravo.text: He came with the post. The Guild hires him out of the Long Stride by the season. He sits on the steps with his hand on his hilt in case anybody counts differently. — He was hired by the same people who hired my predecessor. I think about that more than I would like.

q_tithe_day_offer.speaker: Wystan Crail
q_tithe_day_offer.text: — You can tell. Of course you can; it's on my face; my mother said so. — My predecessor kept two books. One for the Guild at one in ten, and one in brown ink at one in eight, and the difference is a tidy sum in a margin that goes nowhere. Oulea, mostly. The Hurdles. — Reedfolk always keep their own count. The trappers will have a stick, notched, every barrel. If I had it I would know which book is the lie. — I can't go myself. If I leave the desk, the gentleman on the steps will want to know where, and I'd rather he didn't.

choices.text: I'll find the trappers' stick at the Hurdles.
Not now.

q_tithe_day_accept.speaker: Wystan Crail
q_tithe_day_accept.text: Thank you. — The Hurdles are out west, off Oulea, a raft of huts among the wattle. The trappers come ashore only for burials, so you'll have to go to them. — Don't mention the Guild. Or do, and see what they say. I'd like to know that too.

q_tithe_day_decide.speaker: Wystan Crail
q_tithe_day_decide.text: — Let me see. — Four hundred and forty. — Forty barrels. Every year for eleven years, the same forty, and they knew, and said nothing, because saying things to the Guild costs more than eels. — I have the stick in my hands and the gentleman on the steps has just stood up. — Tell me what you'd do. I have been a clerk for nine years and nobody has ever asked me to decide anything, and I find I'd like someone else to go first.

choices.text: Put it in the book. The Guild pays back what was taken.
Break the stick. No stick, no forty barrels owed.
It goes back to Oulea. Let them read it out on tithe-day, in front of everyone.
Let me think on it.

q_tithe_day_decide_true_count.speaker: Wystan Crail
q_tithe_day_decide_true_count.text: In the book. Both books; I'll bind the brown one in behind the true one, so the Row can see what it's paying back for. — The gentleman on the steps has sat down again. I think he's waiting to see what the Row says. So am I.

q_tithe_day_decide_break_the_stick.speaker: Wystan Crail
q_tithe_day_decide_break_the_stick.text: — … — It broke very easily. Eleven years, and it broke like a withy. — The book agrees with itself. The Row will be pleased. — Here. The Guild's gratitude, which I'm authorised to give in marks and not in any other form.

q_tithe_day_decide_back_to_oulea.speaker: Wystan Crail
q_tithe_day_decide_back_to_oulea.text: Read it out. In front of all three landings. — I'll have to write down what they say. In the book. — Oh. That's rather good. That's rather good, isn't it. The book will have to say it.

notes: The tender of Isse's Chair; the naming-cord; Isse of the Reeds (WORLD_BIBLE 1.5, the Named).

greetings.text: Hester Wrenn came and stood between the stilts, where she was married, and said her own name, and asked me to tie it. A loop and a knot, and then she made me undo the loop. Not yet, she said. I have never had to untie one before.
Still carrying your knot? Good. It will not rot. None of mine do.

greet.speaker: Maue Oul
greet.text: Mind the reeds; they are somebody's. — You came to look at the stilts. Everybody comes to look at the stilts. Oul. Maue. I tend the Chair, which means I tie, and I clear the seat, and I stand in the middle when two people cannot agree who holds which end of a reed.

hub.speaker: Maue Oul
hub.text: Ask while my hands are busy. I listen better tying.

choices.text: Whose stilts are these?
What is the seat made of?
What is on the naming-cord?
There's a knot on the seat in no weave you know.
Would you tie my name?
I'll leave the Chair be.

isse.speaker: Maue Oul
isse.text: Isse's. The first house on legs. — Before Isse the reedfolk lived on heaps of stone in the water, like the old crannog, and drowned every spring flood. Isse walked down the Builders' stair into the water and along the bottom to the leaning house, and came back up with the stilts. These are the legs of the house she built after. Bog-oak, turned to stone at the foot where the water keeps them. — She sat on the seat and taught the others. That is why it is a chair and not an altar. We do not have altars. We have somewhere to sit and learn.

the_seat.speaker: Maue Oul
the_seat.text: Builders' stone, green, like the Nave. Older than the stilts; the stilts were driven round it. Nobody knows why a woman who taught the reedfolk to live on legs sat down on a Builders' stone to do it, and I have stopped being asked, because I say: because it was there, and it was dry.

the_cord.speaker: Maue Oul
the_cord.text: Every name said here. Married, two knots twisted together. Dead, a knot and a loop. Born, a knot and nothing, because nothing has happened to them yet. — Eleven thousand, near enough. I can read them all back. — Except the first. Pale green rush that does not grow in the Delta, like it was cut out of the seat. A born knot. — That is Isse. Nothing has happened to her yet.

the_strange_knot.speaker: Maue Oul
the_strange_knot.text: — You saw it. — It is a born knot. In green rush. Like the first on the cord. It was on the seat a month ago one morning, and it has not rotted in a month of rain. — I have not tied it on. I do not know whose it is to tie. — If you want my guess, and you should not, it is the same hand as the first. Something has happened to her at last.

your_name.speaker: Maue Oul
your_name.text: Give me your name. — No, I heard. — There. Your weave. Keep it on you. When you go into the water, or into the ground, or into the grey, whoever finds you will know you were said once, at the Chair, by somebody who meant it.

bye.speaker: Maue Oul
bye.text: Walk out between two stilts, not past them. It is only manners.

notes: The Leech-Wife's Stilts; gives core:quest/the_old_bitch (the collar is delivered to her by the next conversation, QuestLog._hand_over).

greetings.text: The collar's on its hook. The young ones came to the door last night instead of the tubs. I let the two pups in. Don't tell anybody; I'm a hard woman.
You've got her collar. I can hear it on you. Give it here.

greet.speaker: Illa Nauve
greet.text: Don't stand there. That's tub three, and they're the old ones, and they like warm. — Nauve. Illa. The leech-wife. If you're bleeding I'll sell you something for it; if you're not, I'll sell you something anyway, that's trade.

choices.text: Who buys leeches?
What are the collars on the pole?
Your hounds went wild?
I'll be going.

leeches.speaker: Illa Nauve
leeches.text: Isseva's bleeders, the Council when it's feeling its age, and the Tollmere barbers when the Guild boat's in. Black-backs for bad blood, striped for bruising. — They're patient things. Reedfolk virtue. They wait till you've forgotten them and then they drink. I like them better than most people.

collars.speaker: Illa Nauve
collars.text: The hounds'. Reed, Rope, Sallow, Lantern, Bittern, three pups not named, and Mother. — I bred them to keep the herons off the tubs. A hound bitten by a leech learns to bite like one; takes a mouthful, lets go, waits. Good against herons. — Mother's hook is the empty one. Look at the scratches under it. Something's been pulling at it from below.

q_the_old_bitch_offer.speaker: Illa Nauve
q_the_old_bitch_offer.text: At the thaw Mother slipped her collar and went into the reeds, and the rest went after her. She's old. She was going somewhere to die, I reckon, and they wouldn't let her go alone. — Only she didn't die. She found something in the withies that suited her, and now they lie up in the Withy Beds by day, and at night they come for the tubs, and not the door. Not once the door. — Put her down. She'd want it done by somebody who meant it. And bring me her collar. It goes on its hook.

choices.text: I'll go to the Withy Beds.
Not now.

q_the_old_bitch_accept.speaker: Illa Nauve
q_the_old_bitch_accept.text: By day. They lie up in the thick stools at the east end. The young ones will come at you first; she'll hang back in the reeds and wait for you to drop your guard. She taught them that. I taught her.

notes: Peat-cutter at the Peat Hags (the kept Warden, core:quest/the_slow_reflection's 'between').

greetings.text: Stay by the fire. The hounds come up to the cuttings after dark. They want the Warden, I think. Everything wants the Warden.

greet.speaker: Deo Oul
greet.text: Don't touch that stack, you'll have it over. — Oul. Deo. Peat for Isseva and half of Tollmere's back streets, and whatever's in the peat for whoever pays more, which is always somebody, which is a disgrace.

choices.text: What do you find in the peat?
Why do you stack them like loaves?
I'll let you get on.

finds.speaker: Deo Oul
finds.text: Pins. Bowls. A dog with its collar on, which we put back. — And a Warden, in his coat, perfectly kept, with a roll of names in his hand. The Wardens want him and the Order wants him and nobody wants to pay for him, so he's under a tarpaulin by the fire, and my sister talks to him. — It's all in the finds-book on the board by the stacks, with what we're owed. We're owed a lot. We'll never see it.

loaves.speaker: Deo Oul
loaves.text: Because they dry better, and because my mother did, and because a turf stacked any other way looks like a turf and a turf stacked like a loaf looks like somebody's going to eat tonight. — People buy the loaves first. It's not the peat. It's the stack.

bye.speaker: Deo Oul
bye.text: Mind the cuttings. They're deeper than they look, and they don't give things back.

notes: Peat-cutter at the Peat Hags who found the kept Warden and talks to him.

greetings.text: The Sayer's readings are done. He was lying right between the two waters, she says, the Warden. I told him. He didn't seem surprised.

greet.speaker: Lia Oul
greet.text: Shh. — Not you. I was telling him about the weather. — Oul. Lia. I keep the finds-book, and I found him. He was holding names. You don't just leave a man who died holding names in a hole.

hub.speaker: Lia Oul
hub.text: He likes company. So do I, a little.

choices.text: Who was the Warden?
Does he answer?
Goodbye, Lia.

the_warden.speaker: Lia Oul
the_warden.text: A Warden of the Hearth, in the old coat, the grey one. The roll in his hand is names from a Vale village I've never heard of; there are thirty on it, and the last one is his, in a different hand, like somebody wrote him in after. — The Order wants him because they say the peat kept him the way the Choir keeps its dead. The Wardens want him because he's theirs. I want him to be let alone by the fire until somebody makes up their mind.

answers.speaker: Lia Oul
answers.text: No. — But when I tell him something, the fire leans toward him. Deo says it's the draught. Deo says everything is the draught. — He listens. You can tell when somebody listens.

bye.speaker: Lia Oul
bye.text: Say goodbye to him too. He can't, but he'd like to.

notes: The Unsung Vault's hook: a PoiTouch on the lintel (world/sites/site_exterior.gd, _hook). Tells; the quest is Eune Mor's to give.

look.speaker: The Keepers' knot-cord
look.text: A cord of indigo rush hung from the Builders' black lintel, knotted along its whole length: one knot for every Keeper of the Vault, the oldest gone pale as bone at the top, the newest dark. The last knot has been tied, and then pulled half undone, and left. From the doorway comes a smell of cold wax and wet stone, and no sound at all, which is wrong: the reedfolk say you could always hear the round from the lintel, faintly, three voices, one singer.

choices.text: Leave the cord as it is.

speaker_name: A lantern nailed to the gate
notes: The Stakes at Oulnauve's hook: a PoiTouch at the gate (world/sites/site_exterior.gd, _hook). Tells; the quest is Tuo Lissa's to give.

look.speaker: A lantern nailed to the gate
look.text: A burial lantern, indigo paper on an alder frame, nailed to the gate through its frame with a boat-nail. The oil-well is still full: it was cut from the water before it had burned an hour. On the paper, over the name of whoever it was for, somebody has painted a wave in fresh indigo, and under it: THEY ARE COMING HOME. Behind the stakes, many voices are singing the Tide account, the words in the right order and the tune backwards.

choices.text: Leave it.
